Pathology-05.question: ১) Mumps usually infects
Pathology-05.exp:
Mumps is an acute viral infection caused by the mumps virus (a paramyxovirus) and most commonly affects the parotid salivary glands.

Features:

  • Painful parotid swelling (often bilateral)

  • Fever

  • Malaise

  • Pain on chewing or swallowing

Complications:

  • Orchitis (post-pubertal males)

  • Oophoritis

  • Pancreatitis

  • Aseptic meningitis

  • Encephalitis

Other options:

  • Sublingual gland: Rarely involved.

  • Submandibular gland: May occasionally be affected but much less commonly than the parotid.

  • Buccal gland: Not the typical site of infection.

Exam Pearl:
Mumps → Parotid gland (most commonly bilateral painful parotitis).
Causative organism: Mumps virus (Paramyxoviridae).

Pathology-05.question: ২) Most common tumor of the salivary gland
Pathology-05.exp:
Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common salivary gland tumor and the most common benign salivary gland neoplasm.

Features:

  • Most commonly arises in the parotid gland (~80%).

  • Slow-growing, painless, firm, mobile mass.

  • Composed of epithelial and myoepithelial cells with a mixed stromal (myxoid/chondroid) component.

  • Has a risk of malignant transformation to carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma if left untreated for many years.

Other options:

  • Adenocarcinoma: Malignant but much less common.

  • Warthin tumour: Second most common benign parotid tumour; strongly associated with smoking.

  • Mucoepidermoid carcinoma: Most common malignant salivary gland tumour, but not the most common overall.

Exam Pearl:

  • Most common salivary gland tumour → Pleomorphic adenoma.

  • Most common benign tumour → Pleomorphic adenoma.

  • Most common malignant tumour → Mucoepidermoid carcinoma.

Pathology-05.question: ৩) Clinical features of Achalasia excludes
Pathology-05.option2: Low LES pressure on esophageal Manometry
Pathology-05.option4: Increased risk for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
Pathology-05.exp:
The incorrect (excluded) feature of achalasia is low LES pressure.

In achalasia:

  • There is failure of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES).

  • LES resting pressure is increased (or at least impaired relaxation), not low.

  • There is loss of esophageal peristalsis due to degeneration of the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus.

Other options:

  • ✅ Dysphagia for solids and liquids – Classic presentation from the beginning.

  • ✅ "Bird-beak" sign on barium swallow – Characteristic radiological finding due to tapering of the distal esophagus.

  • ✅ Increased risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma – Long-standing achalasia increases the risk.

Exam Pearl:
Achalasia = "4 A's"

  • Aperistalsis of esophagus

  • Abnormal LES relaxation

  • Air-fluid level with dilated esophagus

  • Avian ("Bird-beak") appearance on barium swallow

Remember: Esophageal manometry is the gold standard for diagnosing achalasia.

Pathology-05.question: ৪) Disease that allows “selective” loss of albumin is?
Pathology-05.exp:
Minimal change disease (MCD) causes selective proteinuria, meaning the urine contains predominantly albumin.

Mechanism:

  • Effacement of podocyte foot processes increases glomerular permeability mainly to albumin, while larger proteins (e.g., immunoglobulins) are relatively retained.

  • It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

  • Patients typically respond well to corticosteroids.

Other options:

  • Diabetes: Causes non-selective proteinuria as nephropathy progresses.

  • Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS): Usually causes non-selective proteinuria and is less steroid-responsive.

  • Hypertension: Causes chronic kidney damage but not selective albumin loss.

Exam Pearl:

  • Selective albuminuria → Minimal change disease.

  • Non-selective proteinuria → FSGS, membranous nephropathy, diabetic nephropathy.

Pathology-05.question: ৫) Most important risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma-
Pathology-05.exp:
Barrett's oesophagus is the most important risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Mechanism:

  • Chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) causes replacement of the normal stratified squamous epithelium by intestinal-type columnar epithelium (intestinal metaplasia).

  • This metaplasia can progress through:

    • Low-grade dysplasia

    • High-grade dysplasia

    • Esophageal adenocarcinoma

Other options:

  • Achalasia cardia: Increases the risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, not adenocarcinoma.

  • Mallory-Weiss tear: A mucosal laceration causing upper GI bleeding; not a premalignant condition.

  • Esophageal fistula: Not a recognized risk factor for adenocarcinoma.

Exam Pearl:

  • Barrett's oesophagus → Esophageal adenocarcinoma.

  • Achalasia, smoking, alcohol → Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

Pathology-05.question: ৬) Most common site of carcinoid tumor-
Pathology-05.exp:
The vermiform appendix is the most common site of gastrointestinal carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumors.

Key facts:

  • Appendix → Most common site overall (often incidental during appendectomy).

  • Small intestine (terminal ileum) → Second most common site and the most common site associated with carcinoid syndrome, especially when liver metastases are present.

Other options:

  • Small intestine: Common, but not the most common overall.

  • Rectum: A recognized site but less common than appendix and small intestine.

  • Stomach: Relatively uncommon and often associated with chronic atrophic gastritis or MEN-1.

Exam Pearl:

  • Most common site of carcinoid tumor → Appendix.

  • Most common malignant carcinoid causing carcinoid syndrome → Terminal ileum (small intestine).

Pathology-05.question: ৭) Crohn's disease causes-
Pathology-05.exp:
Crohn's disease is characterized by deep, linear (longitudinal) ulcers with transmural inflammation.

These deep linear ulcers, together with intervening edematous mucosa, produce the characteristic "cobblestone appearance." Because inflammation is transmural, Crohn's disease may also cause fistulas, strictures, and abscesses.

Other options:

  • ক) Diffuse continuous ulcer– Characteristic of ulcerative colitis, which has continuous mucosal involvement.

  • খ) Superficial ulcer – More typical of ulcerative colitis, where inflammation is limited to the mucosa.

  • ঘ) Submucosal ulcer – Not the characteristic lesion of Crohn's disease.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

Feature Crohn's Disease Ulcerative Colitis
Distribution Skip lesions Continuous
Depth Transmural Mucosa & submucosa
Ulcers Deep, linear Superficial, broad
Appearance Cobblestone Pseudopolyps
Fistula/Stricture Common Rare

Exam Pearl:
Crohn's disease = "Skip lesions + Transmural inflammation + Deep linear ulcers + Cobblestone appearance."

Pathology-05.question: ৮) Most common cause of cirrhosis of liver -
Pathology-05.exp:
Alcoholic liver disease is the most common cause of liver cirrhosis in many traditional MBBS/FCPS examination references (e.g., Davidson). Chronic excessive alcohol intake leads to:

  • Fatty liver → Alcoholic hepatitis → Cirrhosis

  • Progressive fibrosis and regenerative nodule formation

  • Portal hypertension and liver failure

Note: In many countries today, chronic hepatitis B/C and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD/previously NAFLD) are increasingly common causes. However, for standard exam MCQs with these options, Alcoholic cirrhosis is the expected answer.

Other options:

  • Postnecrotic cirrhosis: Usually follows chronic viral hepatitis or massive hepatic necrosis.

  • Biliary cirrhosis: Results from chronic cholestatic liver diseases (e.g., primary biliary cholangitis).

  • Cryptogenic cirrhosis: Cause remains unknown; many cases are now recognized as burnt-out MASLD.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

Cause Typical association
Alcoholic Most common cause of cirrhosis (exam answer)
Postnecrotic Chronic hepatitis B/C
Biliary Chronic cholestatic disease
Cryptogenic Unknown (often burnt-out MASLD)

Exam Pearl:
Alcoholic liver disease is the classic MCQ answer for the most common cause of cirrhosis, whereas chronic hepatitis B is the most common cause in many Asian countries, including Bangladesh.

Pathology-05.question: ৯) Neoplastic polyp of gastrointestinal tract-
Pathology-05.exp:
Tubular adenoma is a neoplastic (adenomatous) polyp of the gastrointestinal tract and is considered a premalignant lesion.

Mechanism:

  • Arises from dysplastic glandular epithelium.

  • Follows the adenoma–carcinoma sequence through accumulation of genetic mutations (e.g., APC mutation).

  • Risk of malignant transformation increases with:

    • Larger size (>2 cm)

    • Villous architecture

    • High-grade dysplasia

Other options:

  • Hyperplastic polyp: Non-neoplastic; negligible malignant potential.

  • Hamartomatous polyp: Non-neoplastic developmental lesion (e.g., Peutz-Jeghers syndrome).

  • Inflammatory polyp: Non-neoplastic; seen in inflammatory bowel disease.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

Polyp type Neoplastic? Malignant potential
Tubular adenoma  Yes Premalignant
Hyperplastic polyp No Minimal
Hamartomatous polyp  No Usually none (syndromic exceptions)
Inflammatory polyp  No None

Exam Pearl:
The most common neoplastic colorectal polyp is the tubular adenoma, whereas the most common malignant GI polyp is adenocarcinoma arising from an adenomatous polyp.

Pathology-05.question: ১০) Floor of bacillary ulcer formed by -
Pathology-05.exp:
Bacillary ulcers (classically seen in bacillary dysentery/Shigella infection) are superficial ulcers that are limited to the mucosa. Therefore, the floor of the ulcer is formed by the muscularis mucosa.

In contrast:

  • Amoebic ulcers are deeper, flask-shaped ulcers extending into the submucosa.

  • Typhoid ulcers may extend deeper, with the floor formed by the muscular coat (muscularis propria).

Other options:

  • ক) Submucous coat: Seen in deeper ulcers such as amoebic ulcers, not typical bacillary ulcers.

  • গ) Muscle coat: Characteristic of deeper ulcers (e.g., typhoid), not bacillary ulcers.

  • ঘ) Peritoneum: Indicates a perforating ulcer, not a typical bacillary ulcer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

Ulcer Depth Floor
Bacillary ulcer Superficial Muscularis mucosa
Amoebic ulcer Flask-shaped, deep Submucosa
Typhoid ulcer Deep Muscularis propria

Exam Pearl:
Bacillary dysentery → superficial mucosal ulcers. Amoebiasis → flask-shaped deep ulcers. Typhoid → longitudinal deep ulcers with risk of perforation.

Pathology-05.question: ১১) Non hepatitic cause of hepatomegaly-
Pathology-05.exp:
CCF is a non-hepatic (extrahepatic) cause of hepatomegaly.

Mechanism:

  • In right-sided heart failure, increased central venous pressure causes passive congestion of the liver (congestive hepatomegaly).

  • Patients may have:

    • Tender enlarged liver

    • Raised JVP

    • Peripheral edema

    • Ascites

Other options:

  • Budd–Chiari syndrome: Hepatic venous outflow obstruction; a primary hepatic vascular disease.

  • Polycystic liver: An intrinsic hepatic disorder causing hepatomegaly.

  • Hydatid cyst: A hepatic parasitic disease that enlarges the liver.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

Cause of hepatomegaly Hepatic / Non-hepatic
CCF ✅ Non-hepatic
Budd–Chiari syndrome Hepatic
Polycystic liver Hepatic
Hydatid cyst Hepatic

Exam Pearl:
Right-sided heart failure → Congestive hepatomegaly ("nutmeg liver") → Classic non-hepatic cause of hepatomegaly.

Pathology-05.question: ১২) Metastatic gastrointestinal tumor-
Pathology-05.exp:
A Krukenberg tumour is a metastatic ovarian tumour, most commonly arising from a primary gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma, especially the stomach (diffuse-type gastric carcinoma). It is characterized histologically by mucin-producing signet-ring cells.

Other options:

  • Cystadenocarcinoma: Primary ovarian epithelial malignancy.

  • Kulchitsky cell tumour: Neuroendocrine (carcinoid/small-cell type) tumour, not a metastatic GI tumour.

  • Adenocarcinoma: Usually refers to a primary gland-forming malignancy.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

Tumour Primary or Metastatic?
Krukenberg tumour ✅ Metastatic ovarian tumour (usually from stomach)
Cystadenocarcinoma Primary ovarian tumour
Kulchitsky cell tumour Neuroendocrine tumour
Adenocarcinoma Usually primary glandular malignancy

Exam Pearl:
Krukenberg tumour = Bilateral ovarian metastasis with signet-ring cells, most commonly from gastric adenocarcinoma.

Pathology-05.question: ১৩) Most common site of pancreatic cancer
Pathology-05.exp:
The head of the pancreas is the most common site of pancreatic carcinoma, accounting for about 60–70% of cases.

Clinical features of carcinoma of the head of pancreas:

  • Painless progressive obstructive jaundice (most characteristic)

  • Dark urine, pale stools

  • Pruritus

  • Weight loss

  • Palpable distended gallbladder (Courvoisier sign)

Other options:

  • Body: Less common; usually presents late with epigastric pain and weight loss.

  • Tail: Least common; often remains asymptomatic until advanced disease.

  • Entire gland: Rare.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

Site Frequency Typical presentation
Head 60–70% (Most common) Painless obstructive jaundice
Body 15–20% Epigastric pain, weight loss
Tail 5–10% Late presentation, abdominal/back pain

Exam Pearl:
Most common site of pancreatic cancer → Head of pancreas.
Head lesion → Obstructive jaundice; Body/Tail lesion → Pain and weight loss without early jaundice.

Pathology-05.question: ১৪) Morphological pictures of peptic ulcer-
Pathology-05.option1: Superficial thin layer of granulation tissue
Pathology-05.exp:
A chronic peptic ulcer has a characteristic four-layered microscopic appearance (from surface to depth):

  1. Superficial layer of necrotic debris ✅

  2. Fibrinoid necrosis

  3. Granulation tissue

  4. Fibrous scar (fibrosis)

Among the given options, the most characteristic morphological picture is the superficial layer of necrotic debris.

Other options:

  • ক) Superficial thin layer of granulation tissue Granulation tissue is present beneath the necrotic layer, not superficially.

  • খ) Base of inflammatory tissue  The ulcer base contains granulation tissue and fibrosis, but this is not the classic superficial morphology.

  • ঘ) Erosion of mucosal surface  This describes an erosion, not a true peptic ulcer (which extends beyond the muscularis mucosa).

High-Yield Rapid Recall

Histology of chronic peptic ulcer (Surface → Deep):

  1. Necrotic debris

  2. Fibrinoid necrosis

  3. Granulation tissue

  4. Fibrous scar

Exam Pearl:
Peptic ulcer = 4 histological layers: Necrotic debris → Fibrinoid necrosis → Granulation tissue → Fibrosis.

Pathology-05.question: ১৫) Common carcinoma occurs in gall bladder-
Pathology-05.exp:
Adenocarcinoma accounts for about 90–95% of all gallbladder cancers, making it the most common histological type.

Risk factors:

  • Gallstones (most important)

  • Chronic cholecystitis

  • Porcelain gallbladder

  • Gallbladder polyps (>1 cm)

  • Salmonella typhi carrier state

Other options:

  • Small cell carcinoma: Rare neuroendocrine tumour.

  • Transitional cell carcinoma: Extremely rare.

  • Squamous cell carcinoma: Uncommon (≈2–10%); more aggressive than adenocarcinoma.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

Gallbladder tumour Frequency
Adenocarcinoma Most common (90–95%)
Squamous cell carcinoma Rare
Small cell carcinoma Very rare
Transitional cell carcinoma Extremely rare

Exam Pearl:
Gallstones are the strongest risk factor for gallbladder adenocarcinoma.
Most common histological type of gallbladder cancer → Adenocarcinoma.

Pathology-05.question: ১৬) Which one is not a cause of primary glomerular nephrotic syndrome-
Pathology-05.exp:
The question asks for the condition that is not a primary glomerular nephrotic syndrome (classically in adult nephrotic syndrome classification).

The major primary causes of nephrotic syndrome are:

  • ✅ Minimal change disease (MCD)

  • ✅ Membranous nephropathy (membranous glomerulopathy)

  • ✅ Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (option গ appears to have a typo: "Membranous segmental glomerulosclerosis" should be Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis).

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is classically a mixed nephritic–nephrotic syndrome and is now more commonly associated with secondary causes (e.g., hepatitis B/C, complement-mediated disease). Therefore, it is the best answer.

Other options:

  • Membranous glomerulopathy: Common primary nephrotic syndrome in adults.

  • Minimal change disease: Most common nephrotic syndrome in children.

  • FSGS: Common primary nephrotic syndrome in adults.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

Primary nephrotic syndrome Typical feature
Minimal change disease Children, steroid responsive
Membranous nephropathy Most common primary cause in adults
FSGS Common in adults; may progress to CKD
MPGN Mixed nephritic–nephrotic; often secondary

Exam Pearl:
Primary nephrotic syndromes = MCD, Membranous nephropathy, FSGS.
MPGN is classically a mixed nephritic–nephrotic disease and is frequently secondary.

Pathology-05.question: ১৭) Radio-opaque renal stone-
Pathology-05.exp:
Calcium oxalate stones are radio-opaque and are the most common type of renal stone (≈70–80%).

Radiological features:

  • Calcium oxalate → Radio-opaque ✅

  • Calcium phosphate → Also radio-opaque

  • Uric acid → Radiolucent

  • Xanthine → Radiolucent (or only faintly opaque)

Since the question asks for a radio-opaque stone, calcium oxalate is the best answer because it is the commonest radio-opaque renal stone.

Other options:

  • Uric acid stone:  Radiolucent.

  • Phosphate stone:  Radio-opaque, but less common than calcium oxalate.

  • Xanthine stone:  Usually radiolucent.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

Stone type X-ray appearance
Calcium oxalate  Radio-opaque
Calcium phosphate  Radio-opaque
Struvite  Radio-opaque
Uric acid  Radiolucent
Xanthine  Radiolucent
Cystine Faintly radio-opaque

Exam Pearl:

  • Most common renal stone → Calcium oxalate.

  • Most common radiolucent stone → Uric acid.

  • Most common radio-opaque stone → Calcium oxalate.

Pathology-05.question: ১৮) Urinary bladder cancer caused by-
Pathology-05.exp:
Schistosoma haematobium is a well-established cause of urinary bladder cancer, particularly squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. The parasite deposits eggs in the bladder wall, leading to chronic inflammation, fibrosis, squamous metaplasia, and eventually malignant transformation. This association is especially common in endemic regions of Africa and the Middle East. In contrast, gonococcal and chlamydial infections primarily cause urethritis and genital tract infections and are not established causes of bladder cancer. Schistosoma mansoni mainly affects the intestinal tract and liver, causing intestinal and hepatosplenic disease rather than urinary tract pathology.

This MCQ is not ambiguous. Although most bladder cancers worldwide are urothelial (transitional cell) carcinomas, the parasitic cause classically tested in examinations is Schistosoma haematobium, which is strongly associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

Pathology-05.question: ১৯) Most common cause of of renal cell carcinoma-
Pathology-05.exp: The question is poorly worded, because renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is itself a group of malignant renal tumors. The most common subtype of RCC is clear cell renal cell carcinoma, also known as conventional (non-papillary) RCC, accounting for approximately 70–80% of all RCCs. It arises from the proximal renal tubular epithelium and is strongly associated with VHL gene abnormalities. Papillary RCC is the second most common subtype (10–15%), while chromophobe RCC accounts for about 5%. Urothelial carcinoma originates from the renal pelvis (urothelium) rather than the renal parenchyma and is therefore not a subtype of RCC. Thus, the single best answer is non-papillary (clear cell) carcinoma.

Pathology-05.question: ২০) Which one is not a feature of of nephrotic syndrome-
Pathology-05.exp:
Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminaemia, generalized edema, hyperlipidaemia, and lipiduria. These findings result from increased glomerular permeability, leading to urinary loss of plasma proteins and compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis. Haematuria is not a typical feature of nephrotic syndrome. Although microscopic haematuria may occur in some glomerular diseases causing nephrotic syndrome (e.g., membranous nephropathy or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis), it is not one of the defining features. Prominent haematuria is more characteristic of nephritic syndrome, which is associated with glomerular inflammation, red blood cell casts, hypertension, and reduced renal function.

This MCQ is not ambiguous. The single best answer is Haematuria.

Pathology-05.question: ২১) Prerenal cause of of acute renal failure-
Pathology-05.exp:
Prerenal acute kidney injury (AKI) results from reduced renal perfusion without intrinsic damage to the renal parenchyma. Renal artery stenosis decreases blood flow to the kidney, leading to reduced glomerular filtration and is therefore classified as a prerenal cause of AKI. In contrast, primary glomerular disease, acute tubular necrosis (ATN), and interstitial disease are all intrinsic (intrarenal) causes of AKI because they directly damage the glomeruli, tubules, or interstitium. Although bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis in a solitary functioning kidney) is the classic setting for AKI, the single best answer among the given options is renal artery stenosis.

Note: The question is slightly simplified. In clinical practice, the commonest prerenal causes are hypovolemia, decreased cardiac output, and systemic hypotension, but among the listed options, renal artery stenosis is the correct answer.

Pathology-05.question: ২২) Which one is not urinary bladder tumor -
Pathology-05.exp: The question is poorly worded, but the single best answer is Epithelial cell tumor because it is not a specific histological type of urinary bladder tumor. The major epithelial tumors of the urinary bladder include urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma (the most common, about 90%), squamous cell carcinoma, and the rare small cell (neuroendocrine) carcinoma. Therefore, transitional cell tumor, squamous cell tumor, and small cell tumor are all recognized bladder tumor types. In contrast, "epithelial cell tumor" is only a broad descriptive term and not a distinct pathological diagnosis or WHO histological subtype.

Pathology-05.question: ২৩) Malignant tumour of urethrae -
Pathology-05.exp: Urothelial carcinoma (formerly called transitional cell carcinoma) is the most common malignant tumor of the urethra, especially in the proximal urethra lined by urothelium. It arises from the urothelial lining and has the highest incidence among primary urethral malignancies. Squamous cell papilloma and transitional cell papilloma are benign epithelial tumors and therefore are not malignant. Adenocarcinoma is a malignant urethral tumor but is much less common than urothelial carcinoma. Hence, among the given options, urothelial carcinoma is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ২৪) Interstitial disease of kidney -
Pathology-05.exp: Pyelonephritis is an interstitial disease of the kidney, characterized by inflammation involving the renal interstitium and tubules, usually due to a bacterial infection. Acute and chronic pyelonephritis are classic examples of tubulointerstitial nephritis. In contrast, glomerulonephritis primarily affects the glomeruli, nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome resulting from glomerular disease rather than an interstitial disorder, and polycystic kidney disease is an inherited cystic disorder of the kidneys, not an interstitial disease. Therefore, pyelonephritis is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ২৫) Electrolyte imbalance in AGN-
Pathology-05.exp: Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN) causes a reduction in glomerular filtration rate (GFR), resulting in impaired excretion of hydrogen ions and retention of metabolic acids. This leads to metabolic acidosis, which is a common acid–base disturbance in significant renal impairment. Patients may also develop hyperkalemia due to reduced potassium excretion, but hypokalemia is not typical. Hypernatremia is uncommon, as sodium and water retention usually cause dilutional effects rather than elevated serum sodium. Metabolic alkalosis is not a feature of AGN. Therefore, among the given options, metabolic acidosis is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ২৬) Most frequent cause of nephrotic syndrome in children-
Pathology-05.exp: Minimal change disease (MCD) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, accounting for approximately 80–90% of cases in those younger than 10 years. It is characterized by diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy, while light microscopy appears essentially normal. Children typically present with heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia, and most respond dramatically to corticosteroid therapy. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a less common cause in children and is associated with steroid resistance. Membranous glomerulopathy is more common in adults, and IgA nephropathy usually presents with recurrent hematuria rather than nephrotic syndrome.

Pathology-05.question: ২৭) Cast cell found in a AGN-
Pathology-05.exp: Red blood cell (RBC) casts are the characteristic urinary finding in acute glomerulonephritis (AGN). They form when red blood cells leak through inflamed glomerular capillaries into the renal tubules and become embedded in Tamm–Horsfall protein, indicating glomerular bleeding. Their presence is highly suggestive of glomerulonephritis. Hyaline casts are nonspecific and may be seen in healthy individuals or dehydration. Granular casts are commonly associated with acute tubular necrosis and other renal parenchymal diseases. Epithelial casts indicate tubular epithelial injury rather than glomerular inflammation. Therefore, RBC casts are the single best answer for AGN.

Pathology-05.question: ২৮) Neuronal tumor of CNS-
Pathology-05.exp: Gangliocytoma is a neuronal tumor of the central nervous system composed of mature ganglion cells. It is a rare, well-differentiated neuronal neoplasm and is classified among neuronal and mixed neuronal-glial tumors. Astrocytoma is a glial tumor arising from astrocytes. Schwannoma originates from Schwann cells of peripheral nerves and is therefore not a neuronal tumor of the CNS. Medulloblastoma is an embryonal CNS tumor and is not classified as a neuronal tumor. Hence, among the given options, gangliocytoma is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ২৯) Commonest glial tumor-
Pathology-05.exp: Astrocytoma is the most common glial tumor of the central nervous system. It arises from astrocytes and includes a spectrum of tumors ranging from low-grade diffuse astrocytoma to glioblastoma (WHO grade 4), the most aggressive astrocytic tumor. Oligodendroglioma and ependymoma are less common glial tumors arising from oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells, respectively. Ganglioglioma is a rare mixed neuronal-glial tumor rather than a purely glial neoplasm. Therefore, astrocytoma is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ৩০) Childhood tumor occurs in cerebellum -
Pathology-05.exp: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor of childhood and most commonly arises in the cerebellum, typically from the midline cerebellar vermis. Children usually present with features of raised intracranial pressure, truncal ataxia, and obstructive hydrocephalus due to fourth ventricular compression. Astrocytoma can also occur in the cerebellum of children, especially pilocytic astrocytoma, but it is usually benign and is not the classic answer when asked about a childhood cerebellar tumor. Oligodendroglioma is typically a cerebral hemispheric tumor in adults, and meningioma is an extra-axial tumor occurring predominantly in adults. Therefore, medulloblastoma is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ৩১) Bacterial cause of meningitis in neonate
Pathology-05.exp: Escherichia coli (E. coli) is one of the most common bacterial causes of neonatal meningitis, particularly strains possessing the K1 capsular antigen. Neonatal meningitis is most commonly caused by Group B Streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria monocytogenes. Among the given options, E. coli is the correct answer. Haemophilus influenzae type b mainly affects infants older than 2–3 months in the absence of vaccination. Neisseria meningitidis is more common in older infants, children, and adolescents, while Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading cause of meningitis beyond the neonatal period. Therefore, E. coli is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ৩২) Glucose level decrease in CSF in case of which meningitis
Pathology-05.exp: Acute pyogenic (bacterial) meningitis characteristically causes decreased CSF glucose because bacteria consume glucose and inflammation impairs glucose transport across the blood–brain barrier. The CSF also shows marked neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and increased opening pressure. In viral meningitis, CSF glucose is usually normal. Tuberculous meningitis also causes low CSF glucose, but if a single best answer is required, acute pyogenic meningitis is the classic and expected choice. Parasitic meningitis generally does not produce the characteristic low CSF glucose seen in bacterial meningitis. Therefore, acute pyogenic meningitis is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ৩৩) Red cell increase in CSF in case of-
Pathology-05.exp: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) characteristically causes an increased red blood cell (RBC) count in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) because blood enters the subarachnoid space. The RBC count remains elevated in sequential CSF tubes, and xanthochromia develops several hours after the hemorrhage due to hemoglobin breakdown. In multiple sclerosis, CSF typically shows oligoclonal bands and mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, not increased RBCs. Pyogenic meningitis is characterized by neutrophilic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose, while tuberculous meningitis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose. Neither condition typically causes an increased CSF RBC count. Therefore, subarachnoid hemorrhage is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ৩৪) Which one is not a lesion of neurosyphilis -
Pathology-05.exp: Neurosyphilis is a manifestation of tertiary syphilis involving the central nervous system. The major recognized forms include meningovascular neurosyphilis, general paresis (paretic neurosyphilis), and tabes dorsalis, each resulting from chronic infection by Treponema pallidum. Meningovascular disease causes chronic meningitis and cerebral infarction, paretic neurosyphilis presents with progressive dementia and personality changes, and tabes dorsalis affects the posterior columns and dorsal roots, causing sensory ataxia and loss of proprioception. Hyperplastic is not a recognized clinical or pathological form of neurosyphilis. Therefore, Hyperplastic is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ৩৫) Degenerative disease affecting cerebral cortex-
Pathology-05.exp: Alzheimer's disease is the most common degenerative disease affecting the cerebral cortex. It is characterized by progressive loss of cortical neurons, particularly in the hippocampus and association cortices, leading to memory impairment, cognitive decline, and dementia. The pathological hallmarks are β-amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein. Parkinson's disease primarily affects the substantia nigra, progressive supranuclear palsy mainly involves the brainstem and basal ganglia, and corticobasal degeneration affects both the cortex and basal ganglia but is much less common and not the classic cortical degenerative disorder. Therefore, Alzheimer's disease is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ৩৬) Demyelinating disease-
Pathology-05.exp: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is the prototype demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (CNS). It is an immune-mediated disorder characterized by destruction of myelin with relative preservation of axons, leading to disseminated plaques in the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerves. Patients present with recurrent neurological deficits such as optic neuritis, sensory disturbances, weakness, and ataxia. Peripheral neuropathy affects peripheral nerves and is not a specific demyelinating disease in this context. Huntington disease is a neurodegenerative disorder involving the basal ganglia caused by CAG repeat expansion, while encephalopathy is a broad term describing diffuse brain dysfunction rather than a demyelinating disorder. Therefore, multiple sclerosis is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ৩৭) Peripheral nerve sheath tumor
Pathology-05.exp: Schwannoma is a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor arising from Schwann cells, which produce the myelin sheath of peripheral nerves. It is usually well-circumscribed, encapsulated, and commonly involves cranial nerves, especially the vestibular division of the eighth cranial nerve (vestibular schwannoma). Neurocytoma is a rare neuronal tumor of the central nervous system, typically occurring within the lateral ventricles. Neuroblastoma is a malignant embryonal tumor derived from neural crest cells, most commonly arising in the adrenal medulla or sympathetic ganglia. Meningioma originates from arachnoid cap cells of the meninges and is not a peripheral nerve sheath tumor. Therefore, Schwannoma is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ৩৮) Gastric metastasis to pouch of Doglas is known as
Pathology-05.exp: Blumer shelf refers to a metastatic deposit of gastric carcinoma in the rectovesical pouch (male) or rectouterine pouch (Pouch of Douglas, female), producing a palpable shelf-like mass on rectal examination. It is a classic sign of advanced intra-abdominal malignancy, particularly gastric cancer. Irish node is metastasis to the left axillary lymph node, Virchow gland (Virchow node) is metastasis to the left supraclavicular lymph node, and Sister Mary Joseph nodule is a metastatic umbilical nodule. Therefore, Blumer shelf is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ৩৯) Most gastric adenocarcinoma involves
Pathology-05.exp: Gastric adenocarcinoma most commonly arises in the antrum (distal stomach), particularly in regions with a high prevalence of Helicobacter pylori infection and the intestinal type of gastric cancer. Chronic H. pylori gastritis can progress through atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, and finally adenocarcinoma. Although the incidence of cardia gastric adenocarcinoma has increased in some Western countries, especially in association with obesity and gastroesophageal reflux disease, the antrum remains the classic and expected answer in standard undergraduate and postgraduate medical examinations. Therefore, antrum is the single best answer.

Pathology-05.question: ৪০) Common site of local invasion of gastric carcinoma excludes
Pathology-05.exp: Gastric carcinoma commonly spreads by direct local invasion into adjacent structures. Frequently involved sites include the duodenum, pancreas, transverse colon, omentum, and the retroperitoneum in advanced disease. The jejunum is anatomically separated from the stomach by the duodenum and is not a common site of direct local invasion. Therefore, among the given options, jejunum is the single best answer as the site excluded from common local invasion by gastric carcinoma.

Pathology-05.question: ৪১) Colorectal carcinoma peaks at age
Pathology-05.exp: Colorectal carcinoma is predominantly a disease of older adults, with the peak incidence between 60 and 70 years of age. Although the risk begins to increase after 50 years, the highest frequency occurs in the sixth and seventh decades of life. Major risk factors include increasing age, adenomatous polyps, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), Lynch syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, smoking, and diets high in red and processed meat. While the incidence of early-onset colorectal cancer is increasing, it remains much less common than disease occurring in older individuals. Therefore, 60–70 years is the single best answer.

৪৭) Most frequent presentation of RPGN
Pathology-05.exp: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is a clinical syndrome characterized by rapid loss of renal function with crescent formation in the glomeruli. Among the given options, IgA nephritis (IgA nephropathy) is the most frequent cause associated with an RPGN presentation. However, the most common overall cause of RPGN varies by population, with pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis (ANCA-associated vasculitis) being a major cause. Post-infectious glomerulonephritis can rarely present as RPGN, while Goodpasture syndrome is an anti-GBM disease and an important but less common cause. Minimal change disease does not typically cause RPGN. Therefore, among the given options, IgA nephritis is the best answer.
